parsed.explanation: Combined national-plus-division regime is High Risk. National rules make passport/visa markers sex-at-birth, stop X processing, permit refusal on sex doubt and possible lifetime fraud ineligibility; advisories and detentions follow. The division criminalises restroom/changing-room use not matching birth sex in government buildings and public-facing private businesses, first offence up to a year, with no resolved injunction or enforcement record. National immigration/corrections custody shows severe abuse. Partial hate-crime coverage and pending litigation are not operative traveller protections. There is no general criminalisation of trans identity or execution pathway, so above the 0.15 imprisonment-standard anchors, but universal facility criminal exposure and hostile entry place it below 0.25/0.35 denial-with-remedy anchors.

entry_documents.exposure: National passport/visa rules require sex assigned at birth; X processing stopped; discrepancy or reasonable doubt on sex permits refusal and demands for evidence. Suspected wilful misrepresentation can support lifetime fraud ineligibility. Foreign governments issued advisories after detentions.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; fraud finding requires four elements and is not automatic; litigation challenges the passport policy.
entry_documents.interaction: A foreign passport checked at entry can trigger secondary screening and refusal, especially where marker or presentation differs; division X driver licences diverge from national passport rules.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse of transgender men; national corrections policy adopted from 2026 removes hormones and imposes psychiatric substitution; transgender prisoner counts stopped in 2025.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A document or fraud inquiry at the border can move into immigration detention, where the documented custody harms apply; criminal enforcement of the division bathroom law can also lead to local custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law effective 1 July 2026 makes it a crime for a transgender person to use a restroom or changing room not matching birth sex in government buildings and public-facing private businesses including restaurants, gas stations, entertainment venues and hospitals; first offence misdemeanour, up to one year. National order bars federal single-sex facilities congruent with identity.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division law is under constitutional challenge filed 30 April 2026; no enforcement action against a visitor identified; many states have no mapped facility ban.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: An outed visitor in the division faces criminal exposure at ordinary private-business and hospital restrooms; national facilities order adds federal sites.

care_services.exposure: Division bathroom law reaches hospitals, exposing patients in wards and restrooms; national policy restricts gender-affirming care, proposes insurance exclusions for minors, and division law compels medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days.
care_services.protection: No visitor-specific care access or HRT import protection documented; national hate-crime statute does not address care.
care_services.interaction: Emergency or routine care can out a visitor through facility use or disclosure; an adult travelling with a transgender minor faces compelled parental disclosure and restricted care.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' violent groups; justice department reward guidance uses 'radical gender ideology'; official hostility can chill police protection and embolden enforcement against visible trans people.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; counterterrorism strategy states it will not target mere disagreement.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Police are simultaneously a potential recourse and the enforcement actor for the division bathroom law; threat-framing may affect how complaints or visible advocacy are treated.

minors_guardians.exposure: Division law requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days; national executive order directs investigation and prosecution of teachers who use preferred names or pronouns; bathroom law applies to minors.
minors_guardians.protection: Division law is under challenge; no visitor-family protection documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: An adult travelling with a transgender minor faces facility criminal exposure plus compelled disclosure by medical or childcare actors; national school policy pressures staff over names and pronouns.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific data showing transgender violence materially above the general homicide rate; national hate-crime coverage is partial, with only 23 states covering gender identity in bias statutes; official threat-framing may deter reporting.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National gender-identity hate-crime statute exists; some states and localities have protections; no documented pattern of visitor-targeted violence.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: If assaulted, recourse is uneven; if reported for bathroom use, police are the enforcement actor rather than protector.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Division bathroom law is effective and challenged but not enjoined; national passport restrictions are in litigation; enforcement record absent; sources differ on misdemeanour versus felony classification.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-rights suit filed 30 April 2026; national passport suits; legal-aid FAQ; existing X passports valid until expiry.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A traveller cannot rely on an operating remedy at the point of encounter; the division law's effect and the national passport policy's final scope remain unresolved.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.15-A involves severe multi-year imprisonment as the standard outcome for a foreign national after document mismatch. Here there is no general imprisonment standard for trans identity at the border, but the division criminalises facility use with up to a year and national custody abuse is documented. Slightly less severe overall, hence above 0.15 but still high risk.

0.25-A has invasive administrative review and denial of entry without detention. Here the division adds universal criminal exposure in private-business restrooms and hospitals, plus documented national custody abuse. This is worse than 0.25-A, so the rating sits below it.

0.35-A resolves a document discrepancy through an ombudsman and release without detention. Here no working remedy is documented: the bathroom law is effective and challenged, national entry refusal and fraud risk persist, and custody harms are documented. Materially below 0.35-A.

0.55-B has an operative non-discrimination code and a manager who invokes it to secure service. Here no equivalent traveller-facing protection operates; the division bathroom law and national threat-framing create criminal and official exposure. Far below 0.55-B.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller encounters one system: a foreign passport may trigger national secondary screening or refusal; in the division, any ordinary restroom stop at a restaurant, gas station or hospital is criminalised if birth sex is known, and police are the enforcement actor. A minor in the party faces the same facility exposure plus compelled disclosure by medical, childcare or school actors under division law, while national policy pressures teachers over names and pronouns. Custody, if entered through immigration or criminal process, carries documented abuse. Hate-crime law and litigation exist but do not reliably protect a visitor at the point of encounter. Hence severe but not near-certain imprisonment or execution.
